blocks.content: The dns-resolution-flow topic walked through the full root, TLD, authoritative server chain, and even briefly mentioned that checking a cache is the actual first step. This topic goes deep into exactly how that caching works, and why it is genuinely essential to keeping the entire global DNS system fast and functional at all.
Without caching, DNS simply could not work at the scale the real internet operates at. This topic explains precisely why, and the specific mechanism, TTL, that makes it all work correctly.
/engineering/library/cn/images/1785437576027-531419148.png
1. Why Caching Is Not Optional, It Is Essential
blocks.text: 1. Why Caching Is Not Optional, It Is Essential

blocks.content: Without caching, every single DNS lookup, for every single request, from every single device on the entire planet, would need to repeat the ENTIRE multi step resolution chain covered in the resolution flow topic, root server, TLD server, authoritative server, every single time. The relatively small number of root and TLD servers would be instantly overwhelmed by this sheer volume, many, many times over.
/engineering/library/cn/images/1785437576027-854163404.png
blocks.alt: Why Caching Is Not Optional, It Is Essential

blocks.content: 2. Caching Happens at Multiple Layers at Once
blocks.text: 2. Caching Happens at Multiple Layers at Once

blocks.content: Caching is not just one single thing happening in one single place. Your browser keeps its own small cache. Your operating system keeps its own separate cache. Your recursive resolver, from the resolution flow topic, keeps a much larger cache serving many users at once. A fresh lookup only ever needs to go all the way to the authoritative chain if every single one of these layers comes up empty.

3. TTL: How Long an Answer Stays Trustworthy
blocks.text: 3. TTL: How Long an Answer Stays Trustworthy

blocks.content: Every single DNS record carries its own TTL, time to live, value, a specific number of seconds that record is considered safe to cache and reuse before it needs to be looked up fresh again. This value is set by whoever manages the domain DNS records, giving them direct control over this exact tradeoff.
/engineering/library/cn/images/1785437673709-401495741.png
blocks.alt: TTL: How Long an Answer Stays Trustworthy

blocks.content: 4. What Happens When a TTL Expires
blocks.text: 4. What Happens When a TTL Expires

blocks.content: While a cached answer TTL is still valid, it gets served instantly, with zero network lookup at all. The moment that TTL expires, the very next request for that same domain triggers a completely fresh lookup, walking through the resolution chain again and caching the new answer with a fresh TTL of its own.
/engineering/library/cn/images/1785437673709-854933042.png
blocks.alt: What Happens When a TTL Expires

blocks.content: 5. A Worked Example

A record set with a TTL of 3600 seconds, exactly one hour, will be served directly from cache for up to a full hour after it is first looked up, with no repeat network lookup needed during that entire window. Once that hour passes, the next request for that domain triggers a brand new lookup, and the cycle repeats.

6. The Real Tradeoff: Long TTL Versus Short TTL
blocks.text: 6. The Real Tradeoff: Long TTL Versus Short TTL

blocks.content: A long TTL is efficient, dramatically reducing the total number of real lookups needed across the whole internet, but it means a genuine change to a domain record takes longer to actually reach everyone, since existing cached copies keep being used until they naturally expire. A short TTL reflects a real change much faster, but costs more frequent lookups, more real load on the resolution chain.
/engineering/library/cn/images/1785437673710-609139425.png
blocks.alt: The Real Tradeoff: Long TTL Versus Short TTL

blocks.title: There is no universally correct answer
blocks.content: The right TTL genuinely depends on the specific situation. A record that almost never changes can safely use a long TTL for maximum efficiency, while a record expected to change soon benefits from a shorter TTL, accepting the extra lookup cost in exchange for faster propagation.
7. A Real World Application: Planning Ahead for a Migration
blocks.text: 7. A Real World Application: Planning Ahead for a Migration

blocks.content: An organization planning a server migration in advance can deliberately lower a domain TTL well before the actual switch happens. Once cached copies with the old, longer TTL naturally expire and get replaced by fresh copies carrying the new, shorter TTL, the actual migration, when it finally happens, propagates out to users dramatically faster, since the shorter TTL means far fewer stale, outdated cached entries lingering around at that critical moment.
/engineering/library/cn/images/1785437673710-691311680.png
blocks.alt: A Real World Application: Planning Ahead for a Migration

blocks.title: A common real world operations tactic
blocks.content: Teams planning a major infrastructure change routinely lower TTL days in advance specifically for this reason, letting the shorter TTL fully propagate before the actual change happens, so almost nobody is left holding a stale, outdated cached answer at the critical moment.
8. Common Mistakes and Key Takeaways

Setting an unnecessarily short TTL out of caution, when this creates real, avoidable extra lookup load without providing any actual benefit for a record that rarely changes.
